title: How India’s delay is set to leave Rs135m of Nepal’s electricity unsold daily - The Kathmandu Post
description: How India’s delay is set to leave Rs135m of Nepal’s electricity unsold daily  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal risks being left with hundreds of megawatts of surplus electricity each day after failing to secure timely approval from India to sell power through its energy exchange, following the expiry of existing export arrangements.

The inability to export power translates into an estimated Rs135.82 million in potential daily revenue loss for the state-owned power utility, Nepal Electricity Authority.

The authorisation to export 609 megawatts of electricity supplied to three Indian states expired at the end of October. NEA has traditionally shifted such exports to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) after its medium-term power sale agreements expire. But India has yet to approve the arrangement this year, leaving Nepal unable to sell the electricity through the exchange.

NEA Managing Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha said the utility had submitted a proposal to convert the existing arrangements into exchange-based exports in August, but had received no approval from the Indian side despite nearly three months having passed.

Under bilateral agreements, Nepal has been exporting 404MW to Haryana and another 205MW to Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, bringing the total to 609MW.

Bangladesh exports also come to a halt

An additional 40MW of electricity supplied to Bangladesh under a seasonal arrangement has also stopped after the export period expired on Sunday. Nepal has been exporting power to Bangladesh annually between June 15 and November 15.

With exports of 609MW to India and 40MW to Bangladesh on hold, the NEA stands to lose an estimated Rs135.82 million in potential daily revenue, based on an average export rate of 5.45 Indian rupees per unit. The estimated loss is equivalent to around INR84.88 million per day, or approximately Rs135.82 million in Nepali currency.

Nepal currently has approval to export around 1,169MW of electricity to India and Bangladesh. Of this, 649MW is covered by medium-term bilateral agreements and 521MW by sales through the Indian Energy Exchange. Converting the electricity covered by bilateral agreements to exchange-based sales would allow Nepal to export more power whenever domestic generation exceeds demand.

The NEA has been selling surplus electricity generated during the monsoon through the IEX’s day-ahead and real-time markets, where prices are determined competitively. Under the bilateral medium-term agreements, it also supplies electricity to Indian states of Haryana, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh.

An NEA official blamed the current situation on the failure of senior officials at the Energy Ministry and the utility to act effectively and in time, despite knowing that the export authorisation would expire in October. Shrestha, however, said the utility had already sent a request in August to convert the 649MW covered by medium-term arrangements into exchange-based exports.

According to the NEA, the country is currently generating between 2,600MW and 2,700MW against domestic demand of around 2,200MW to 2,300MW. Consumption has also remained relatively low because businesses and factories have yet to resume full operations after the Chhath festival, leaving the utility with a growing surplus that it cannot readily sell.

Not all surplus electricity can be exported, however. Shrestha said the utility must keep around 200MW to 300MW in reserve to maintain system security and prevent disruptions to domestic supply if a major power plant suddenly goes offline.

Such reserves are essential in case of an unexpected outage at a large facility such as the 456 MW Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Project, he said.

Electricity generation and export volumes are typically higher during the monsoon, when rivers carry greater volumes of water. But river flows begin to decline from November-end, reducing hydropower generation and the amount available for export.

What happened

Nepal is preparing to allow India to use its eastern airspace for international flights operating to and from Bagdogra Airport, while Kathmandu continues to seek Indian approval for an additional air route to Bhairahawa.

A government delegation led by Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal Director General Mukesh Dangol held preliminary discussions on the matter in New Delhi two days before the report. A high-level government source said India proposed, during diplomatic talks, that Nepal allow airspace use for flights to and from both Bagdogra and Raxaul. The Nepali side indicated it could agree to the Bagdogra request.

Tourism and Civil Aviation Minister Ganesh Paudel is scheduled to travel to India on Tuesday for further discussions, and an understanding could also be reached during Prime Minister Balendra Shah's planned visit to New Delhi next week. At India's request, the Tourism Ministry also held talks with Buddha Air on Sunday about operating domestic flights between Janakpur and Bhairahawa. India has not yet given a clear response on air routes for Pokhara International Airport.

title: Nepali Bowlers Shine in Nepal Premier League, Foreigners Lead Batting - Ratopati
description: Nepali Bowlers Shine in Nepal Premier League, Foreigners Lead Batting  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Nepali players have performed impressively in bowling in the league stage of the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) cricket. While Nepali bowlers are prominent in the list of highest wicket-takers, foreign players lead in batting. The performance in the league stage shows that Nepali bowlers have demonstrated competitive ability against foreign players. Three out of the four players jointly at the top of the highest wicket-takers list are Nepali. In batting, foreign batsmen are in the first position in the list of highest run-scorers, with Nepali players in second and third places.

Nepali Players Ahead in Bowling

In the NPL league stage, Kamal Singh Airee and Rijan Dhakal of Chitwan Rhinos, Rahul Yadav of Janakpur Bolts, and Jhandad Khan of Kathmandu Gorkhas are jointly at the top of the highest wicket-takers list. They have all taken 12 wickets each. Kamal Airee, associated with Chitwan, took 12 wickets in 5 innings from 6 matches with an economy rate of 5.72. His best bowling performance this season was taking four wickets for 26 runs. Similarly, Rijan Dhakal, also associated with Chitwan, took 12 wickets in six matches. His best bowling performance this season was taking four wickets for 24 runs. Rahul Yadav of Janakpur took 12 wickets in seven matches. His best bowling performance was taking four wickets for 31 runs. Similarly, Jhandad Khan, a fast bowler from Pakistan associated with Kathmandu, took 12 wickets in seven matches. He took four wickets for 23 runs with an excellent performance.

Foreign Players Lead in Batting

Although Nepali players have shown dominance in bowling, foreign players have taken the lead in batting. By the end of the league stage, Yuvraj Samra, a Canadian batsman associated with Pokhara Avengers, is at the top of the list of highest run-scorers. He has scored 294 runs in four matches. Samra batted in 4 innings, maintaining an average of 73.50 and a strike rate of 179.26. His personal highest score is 102 runs. Yuvraj has played one century and two half-centuries in the tournament. Among Nepali batsmen, Lokesh Bam, associated with Biratnagar Kings, has been the most successful in this NPL. He is in second place in the overall list. Lokesh has scored 242 runs in 7 matches. His highest score is 87 runs. Lokesh has played two half-centuries this season. He has scored runs at an average of 34.57 with a strike rate of 142.35. Similarly, Kushal Bhurtel of Pokhara Avengers is in third place with 235 runs. He has scored runs in seven matches at an average of 33.57 and a strike rate of 148.73. His personal highest score is 99 runs. Kushal, who came close to a century, has played two half-centuries in the tournament. Similarly, Rashid Khan, associated with Kathmandu Gorkhas, has scored 186 runs in seven matches. His average is 37.20 and his strike rate is 141.98. Rashid has played two half-centuries in this edition of the NPL. Similarly, Ravi Bopara from England, associated with Chitwan Rhinos, has scored 184 runs in 5 matches. He has played one half-century batting at an overall average of 46. Ravi's highest score is 55 runs.

Nepali Batsmen Awaiting a Century

The difference between foreign and Nepali players is also evident in terms of centuries in the league stage batting statistics. While Yuvraj Samra, who is at the top of the highest run-scorers list, has hit a century, Nepali batsmen are far from achieving this feat. Lokesh Bam reached 87 runs and Kushal Bhurtel reached 99 runs but failed to score a century. Although there have been good individual starts, the challenge for Nepali batsmen is to convert them into big scores.

title: Nepal pushes for recognition of Himalayan crisis as COP31 enters decisive second week - myRepublica
description: Nepal pushes for recognition of Himalayan crisis as COP31 enters decisive second week  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
ANTALYA, November 17: As the second week of the UN climate conference begins in Antalya, Nepal is stepping up diplomatic efforts to secure international recognition of the vulnerabilities of mountain regions, while the broader negotiations remain caught between developing countries' demands for climate finance and developed countries' reluctance to commit additional resources.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

The first week of COP31, which began on November 9, produced progress on several technical and procedural issues, but left the most politically contentious questions unresolved. Climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, emissions reduction and the future of the energy transition remain among the major areas of disagreement.

The conference, widely presented as an implementation-focused COP, was expected to move beyond repeated political declarations and accelerate the delivery of commitments already made under the Paris Agreement. However, negotiations have exposed a familiar divide: developing countries want predictable, grant-based financial support to implement climate action, while developed countries remain reluctant to accept specific public financing obligations. Fossil fuel-producing countries, meanwhile, oppose stronger language on phasing out coal, oil and gas.

Climate activist and Nepal delegate Sanot Adhikari, in his assessment of the first week's proceedings, identified climate finance, the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA), the Loss and Damage Fund, mitigation and energy transition, and carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as the principal areas of discussion. He noted that while some positive initiatives had emerged, major disagreements persisted over how commitments would be financed and implemented.

The second week is therefore expected to be decisive, with ministers and senior political representatives arriving to resolve issues that technical negotiators have been unable to settle. Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who leads the negotiations, has indicated that a draft overarching decision would be circulated early this week, followed by intensive ministerial consultations. The conference is scheduled to conclude on November 20.

Nepal's mountain agenda: A procedural opening, but no breakthrough yet

For Nepal, the most important diplomatic initiative at COP31 has been its attempt, jointly with Bhutan, to establish mountain climate vulnerability as a formal subject of the UN climate process.

Related story Harjeet Singh slams developed nations over failure to put Himal...

However, the proposal did not secure a separate formal agenda item when the COP adopted its agenda on November 9. Instead, the title was broadened to 'Matters Relating to Mountains and Climate Change', with the presidency agreeing to continue consultations and convene mountain-related dialogues at the 66th and 68th sessions of the subsidiary bodies in 2027 and 2028.

Nepal welcomed the compromise but made clear that it fell short of its expectations.

Avishek Shrestha, adviser to Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary, who is also a part of Nepal's delegation, explained that the mountain proposal was not abandoned but shifted into a continuing political and negotiating process in the remaining days of the conference.

"We did not walk away empty handed," Shrestha told Republica describing the revised arrangement as an opportunity to continue pushing for a dedicated mountain agenda.

Nepal's immediate concern is now the wording of the conference's final cover decision. A draft discussed on November 13 recognised the urgency of climate impacts, including those affecting mountains, and called for a dedicated mountain work programme to address finance and capacity-building gaps.

Nepal, Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan submitted further proposals on November 14, seeking explicit language on the programme's scope and modalities, stronger scientific assessments, early warning systems, risk preparedness and the integration of mountain-specific indicators into adaptation and climate finance frameworks.

Nepal also wants the annual mountain dialogues to operate under the proposed work programme rather than remain isolated discussions.

Minister Chaudhary held high-level meetings with Australia's Chris Bowen and Türkiye's chief negotiator Murat Kurum on November 15 to press these demands. According to Shrestha, both sides indicated support and agreed to consider Nepal's concerns in the evolving outcome text.

Why the negotiations remain difficult

The principal obstacle is the consensus-based nature of UN climate negotiations. Unlike institutions where decisions can be taken through majority voting, the UNFCCC process generally requires agreement among participating countries. A single country's objection can therefore delay or block a proposed decision.

Shrestha has acknowledged that Nepal has not yet secured the level of international solidarity it had hoped for, despite approaching different negotiating blocs, including the G77 and China, the Least Developed Countries, the African Group, the Arab Group and European countries.

The wider negotiations face similar difficulties.

Climate finance remains one of the biggest fault lines. Developing countries are demanding delivery of the $300 billion annual climate finance goal by 2035 agreed at COP29 in Baku, alongside a broader effort to mobilise $1.3 trillion annually by that year. They also want the commitment to triple adaptation finance translated into clear implementation arrangements.

However, disagreements persist over the balance between public and private finance, the responsibilities of developed countries and the accessibility of funding for vulnerable nations.

The Gloabal goal on adaption (GGA) negotiations are also facing difficulties over indicators, measurement and financing. Developing countries want adaptation progress to be assessed through practical indicators reflecting the needs of vulnerable communities, rather than merely through national reporting exercises.

On mitigation, the debate over transitioning away from fossil fuels remains contentious. While several countries and coalitions are advancing voluntary clean-energy initiatives and electrification, there is no consensus on stronger negotiated language requiring a phase-out of fossil fuels.

Progress has also been reported in technical discussions on carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, although questions of implementation, transparency and institutional capacity remain important for developing countries.

title: Is Nepal’s new Parliament building ready for winter session move-in? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Is Nepal’s new Parliament building ready for winter session move-in?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The construction of Nepal’s new House of Representatives chamber is complete. The entrance leading to it is not.

That mismatch captures the government’s problem as it prepares to hold the winter session in the new building at Singha Durbar, seven years after construction began. The chamber has yet to undergo technical tests or be formally handed over to the Federal Parliament Secretariat, and work on the National Assembly chamber and other parts of the complex continues. The government wants out of the cramped multipurpose hall where lawmakers now meet. The secretariat is not sure it can make the move in time.

Eakram Giri, joint secretary and spokesperson for the Federal Parliament Secretariat, said the lower house chamber needed to undergo technical checks before it could host parliamentary sessions.

“The audio, video and conferencing systems must be tested to ensure they work properly during live parliamentary proceedings,” Giri said. The tests have yet to be conducted because the chamber has not been formally handed over to the secretariat.

The secretariat aims to begin parliamentary proceedings in the new chamber by the end of November. Giri said there would be no obstacles to holding sessions there, provided the facility was handed over on time and passed the required technical tests.

But the entrance to the chamber is still under construction, while work elsewhere in the complex remains incomplete. The secretariat is therefore not yet confident that the winter session can be held in the new building.

Roshan Shrestha, chief of the Special Building Construction Project, said the House of Representatives chamber was ready for use, although work on the National Assembly chamber remained unfinished. The main structural construction across the complex has largely been completed, but interior finishing and other works are still underway.

Overall construction progress stands at 95 percent, Shrestha said. Work slowed during the Dashain and Tihar festivals, while the closure of border crossings disrupted the supply of interior fittings and other materials from China.

The incomplete complex has forced Parliament to continue using temporary facilities seven years after construction began. The multipurpose hall where the House of Representatives currently meets is too cramped for parliamentary proceedings, according to the secretariat. The National Assembly, meanwhile, has been holding meetings in an old Agriculture Committee hall because its designated chamber is not ready.

The Parliament complex is supposed to accommodate four committees under the National Assembly, 10 under the House of Representatives and two joint committees. The shortage of suitable meeting rooms has also made it difficult for parliamentary committees to conduct their meetings.

The project was originally launched to provide a permanent parliamentary complex for the House elected in 2022. The construction contract was awarded on October 3, 2019. But the building remained incomplete even after the House elected in 2026 was formed, forcing the secretariat to hurriedly arrange the multipurpose hall for parliamentary proceedings.

The main construction contract, worth Rs5.67 billion, was awarded to the Tundi-SHEC joint venture. The original deadline was October 2022. After the project failed to meet it, the deadline was extended five times, first to April 2023, then October 2023, April 2024, March 2025 and December 2025. With the work still incomplete, a sixth extension pushed the deadline to February 2027.

Interior work was contracted separately to the KC-Shyamsundar-Baniya joint venture for Rs2.35 billion. The agreement was signed on July 2, 2023, with completion scheduled for mid-July 2024. The deadline was subsequently extended to March 2025, December 2025 and May 2026. After the work remained unfinished, it was extended for a fourth time, to mid-May 2027.

Roofing work, too, remains incomplete. Chainlink Engineering Company secured the separate roofing contract for Rs37.9 million on March 10, 2024. The work has yet to be completed, and the deadline has been extended to mid-May 2027.

Spread across 156 ropanis of land in the Singha Durbar complex, the new parliamentary precinct consists of buildings of up to five storeys. It includes separate chambers for the House of Representatives and National Assembly, a central lobby, offices for senior dignitaries, a library and a museum.

Other structures have been built for parliamentary party offices, parliamentary committees, the Federal Parliament Secretariat, a cafeteria, and press and printing facilities. Infrastructure for parking 476 four-wheelers and 800 two-wheelers has also been completed, along with a building for security personnel.

Dilip Bhandari, director general of the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction, said Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal had instructed officials to prioritise completion of the House of Representatives chamber for the winter session. Construction work had been accelerated following the directive, he said.

title: Nepal’s stolen heritage in focus at ‘Bring Me Home’ festival in Bhaktapur - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s stolen heritage in focus at ‘Bring Me Home’ festival in Bhaktapur  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
For decades, stone and bronze deities stolen from centuries-old shrines across the Kathmandu Valley have surfaced thousands of miles away in Western museums and private collections. A few have been repatriated but hundreds, if not thousands, are still away.

On Saturday, diplomats, conservationists and local heritage custodians gathered in Bhaktapur to confront the loss—and to debate what bringing those artifacts home truly means.

The weeklong ‘Bring Me Home’ festival, organised by the non-profit Namuna Foundation, coincided with the International Day Against Illicit Trafficking in Cultural Property, marked every November 14 under the 1970 UNESCO Convention. Ambassadors from Australia, Switzerland, Norway and Israel attended alongside UNESCO’s representative to Nepal and former Australian envoy Felicity Volk.

Organisers said the title reflects the longing of displaced deities to return to the neighbourhoods where their spiritual identities remain alive. Yet for the traditional community trusts, or guthi s, that have guarded Nepal’s shrines for generations, repatriation is only half the battle. Many recovered statues end up locked behind museum glass in Kathmandu rather than restored to active worship.

“For us, the true home of a deity is the temple or shrine,” said Prashant Mali, an advisor to the Navadurga Bhawani Devi Guthi based in Thecho, Lalitpur. “Keeping them safe in a museum is not bad, but deities require daily worship— nitya puja and aarti .”

Because they are the centre of devotees’ faith, placing them back in their sacred sites with proper security and surveillance is vital, he added.

When an idol vanishes, Mali said, communities improvise by installing replicas or continuing rituals before an empty plinth, though in some neighbourhoods, festivals and daily worship have ground to a halt. Preserving what remains, he added, depends on pairing the elder’s memories and guthi records with modern safeguards like surveillance cameras and stronger diplomatic coordination.

That gap between museum preservation and living faith is central to the festival curated by Shreena Nepal, programme coordinator at Namuna Foundation, under the guidance of Rabindra Puri, who began working in heritage conservation in 2003.

“The people of our country should be aware of this problem,” Puri said at the inauguration, adding that the foundation plans to mark the observance annually to build public pressure against heritage crime. “The return of these identities is a victory for the entire community.”

At the centre of the programme, which runs through November 21, is an exhibition by the Museum of Stolen Art, displaying a curated selection of stone statues that art historian Lain Singh Bangdel documented in 1989 as stolen from Nepal. Alongside live stone-and-wood-carving demonstrations, documentary screenings and a “homecoming of heritages” segment, the exhibition aims to introduce younger Nepalis to the scale of what was taken.

International envoys framed Nepal’s losses as part of broader reckoning over looted cultural property. Jaco du Toit, the UNESCO representative to Nepal, urged embassies to designate focal points to trace claims swiftly, noting that restitution “touches really at the centre of identity and people’s lives and what they believe in.”

Australian Ambassador Simon Ernst pointed to parallel efforts to recover Aboriginal cultural property and ancestral remains held overseas. “It’s not just a movement in Nepal, that movement is going on around the world,” he said. “You’re part of a broader global movement, and all power to you.”

title: New Nepali Ambassador to India Departs for Delhi - Ratopati
description: New Nepali Ambassador to India Departs for Delhi  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
New Nepali Ambassador to India Dr. Nischalnath Pandey is departing for New Delhi today. He is going to Delhi to prepare for Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India.

According to a source from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Pandey has made preparations to assume his responsibilities upon arriving in New Delhi today.

Prime Minister Shah is preparing to visit India on Mangsir 6. Both countries are working to finalize the agenda for the visit. Pandey was appointed ambassador by the President only on Monday.
